content: A sebaceous cyst, also known as a wen, pilar cyst, or keratinizing cyst, is a closed sac or cyst located beneath the skin's surface. It is lined with tissue resembling the infundibulum, the uppermost part of a hair follicle, and is filled with a fatty, white, semi-solid material called sebum. Sebum is produced by sebaceous glands in the epidermis. The terminology surrounding sebaceous cysts can be confusing. While some sources equate sebaceous cysts with epidermoid cysts, others define them based on their origin. Specifically, a true sebaceous cyst originates from sebaceous glands, whereas epidermoid cysts arise from the epidermis, and pilar cysts originate from hair follicles. Despite these distinctions, the terms are often used interchangeably in clinical practice. True sebaceous cysts are relatively rare. Sebaceous cysts commonly appear on the scalp, ears, back, face, and upper arms, though they can develop anywhere on the body except the palms and soles. In males, they frequently occur on the scrotum and chest. These cysts are more prevalent in hairier areas and, over time, may cause localized hair loss on the skin above the cyst. They are typically smooth to the touch, round in shape, and vary in size. They are generally mobile and may contain fibrous tissue, fluids, or a fatty keratinous substance resembling cottage cheese. In some cases, the cyst may contain a viscous, serosanguinous fluid composed of purulent and bloody material. The contents and surrounding capsule of the cyst can be influenced by whether the cyst has been previously infected. Surgical excision is the most effective treatment for sebaceous cysts. This procedure involves removing the cyst and its contents entirely. Techniques include traditional wide excision, minimal excision, and punch biopsy excision. The area is numbed with a local anesthetic, and the cyst is removed through an incision. If the cyst is removed intact, the cure rate is 100%. However, if the cyst ruptures during removal, the remaining fragments may be scraped out and cauterized to prevent recurrence. Infected cysts may require antibiotics or other treatments before excision. A scar will result from the procedure. Non-surgical management of sebaceous cysts includes the application of a heat pad to the cyst for about 15 minutes twice daily over 10 days. This method works by melting the hardened sebum inside the cyst, allowing it to be reabsorbed by the body. This approach is cost-effective and avoids surgical risks but is not suitable for non-sebaceous cysts, as they do not contain the same hardened sebum deposits. Under no circumstances should a cyst be popped, as this can lead to infection of the surrounding tissue. Special caution is advised for cysts in the neck region due to the presence of vital glands and blood vessels. Additionally, some cysts in the genital area may be forms of herpes and require evaluation by a physician. Blocked sebaceous glands, swollen hair follicles, and excessive testosterone production are common causes of sebaceous cysts. Rarely, they may be caused by parasitic infections, such as Dermatobia hominis.
